primary_citation: Cal. Penal Code §502 (Stats. 1988, Ch. 1523; current version through Stats. 2021, Ch. 535)
short_title: Cal. Penal Code §502 — Unauthorized Computer Access; California Parallel to CFAA
one_line_rule: Knowingly accessing any California computer, computer system, or computer network 'without permission' for fraud, data theft, or simple unauthorized access violates §502; civil remedy provides compensatory damages and injunctive relief with no minimum loss threshold required.

case_law.cite: Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2016)
case_law.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case_law.key_rule: After express revocation of permission, continuing access = 'without permission' under §502; §502 and CFAA analyzed in parallel; 'without permission' (§502) = 'without authorization' (CFAA). Binding 9th Circuit precedent.

case_law.cite: WhatsApp Inc. v. NSO Group Technologies Ltd., 17 F.4th 930 (9th Cir. 2021) (jurisdictional ruling)
case_law.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case_law.key_rule: Parallel pleading of §502 + CFAA is standard in California federal court computer crime civil litigation; exploitation of infrastructure to access computer systems = without permission; California nexus for system location regardless of attacker location. Status note: substantive §502/CFAA claims not finally adjudicated as of Aug. 2025.

primary_claims: §502(c)(1): McClaran used SIM swap to execute fraud scheme via unauthorized access to Michael's email, financial, SSA accounts — wrongfully controlling money and data
§502(c)(7): Each unauthorized login to Michael's accounts = separate §502(c)(7) violation — no fraud element or loss threshold required
sim_swap_application.no_loss_threshold_advantage: Unlike CFAA §1030(g), §502(e) has NO $5,000 aggregate loss threshold — any unauthorized computer access is actionable; state-law backstop for cases where CFAA threshold is arguable
sim_swap_application.california_nexus: Michael's email/financial/SSA accounts are hosted on California-based servers (Google, financial institutions, SSA with California nexus); §502 applies regardless of where McClaran was located
sim_swap_application.at_and_t_exposure: AT&T's California-based SIM porting systems were the mechanism of the attack; AT&T's negligent processing of the SIM swap port may constitute §502(c)(7) unauthorized access facilitation; primary AT&T theory is UCL + negligence, with §502 as an additional hook
sim_swap_application.stacking: §502 + CFAA §1030 + SCA §2701 + CIPA §632.7 + Wiretap §2511 are all pled simultaneously; each covers different elements of the same attack chain
sim_swap_application.defendants: Ryan McClaran (primary §502 defendant); co-conspirators who accessed accounts; UCL/§502 claims against AT&T for carrier facilitation
